newsitem.title: TANZANIA: Scandal-hit Rwanda tribunal restarts trial.
newsitem.headline: Scandal-hit Rwanda tribunal restarts trial.

text.p: The scandal-hit international tribunal on Rwanda's 1994 genocide on Friday resumed the trial of a Hutu former government official charged with genocide and crimes against humanity.
The resumption after Thursday's adjournment followed the arrival of key witnesses from the tiny central African nation.
The case has been overshadowed by serious allegations of mismanagement and abuses levelled against the Arusha-based U.N. Rwanda war crimes court.
The trial of Jean-Paul Akayesu, a former mayor in central Rwanda, resumed with the prosecution presenting its first witness, a Tutsi woman, who worked under Akayesu.
Judge Laity Kama of Senegal, chairman of the three-strong panel of judges hearing the case, ruled that the witness be identified only as "K" to protect her.

Akayesu immediately filed an application seeking to change his lawyers for the third time but Kama reserved ruling until next week. But he ordered the prosecution to continue cross-examination of the witness.

Akayesu, 43, is the first suspect to be tried under the U.N.-created tribunal. The prosecution says the crimes were committed between April and June 1994 when an estimated 800,000 Tutsis and moderate Hutus were killed.
He faces life imprisonement, the tribunal's highest penalty, if convicted.

New U.N. Secretary General Kofi Annan on Thursday promised "decisive action" to correct the abuse allegations which threaten to tarnish the name of the court. Annan said he was sending new personnel to clean up the court.

"The moral weight of this body is enormous and those responsible for carrying out that work must meet the highest ethical and professional standards," he said, according to U.N. spokesman Fred Eckhard.
One of the tribunal's own judges joined the attacks on Friday.

"The atmosphere here is no good. It has been poisoned, there is no good cooperation between the staff and it is worse than in any other organisation that I have ever worked in," Lennart Aspegren of Sweden told reporters.
Karl Paschke of Germany, the U.N. inspector general, has prepared a report on the alleged abuses in the tribunal, and Eckhard said Annan would take action once he had a chance to review it.
Eckhard said a new acting chief of administration, Mohammed Said of Ethiopia, had been sent to Arusha last month, replacing George Anderson of Liberia who had left in October.

In addition, Mario Cianci, who holds Italian and U.S. nationality, was going to Arusha soon to temporarily take over personnel. That position is held by Andronico Adede of Kenya, a legal officer who previously worked in New York.

The Arusha controversy is fraught with racial overtones, with European employees complaining that the tribunal's administrators have given jobs to relatives and friends who have no qualifications and discriminated against non-Africans.

Twenty-one people have been indicted by the tribunal including Akayesu. Eight suspects are still at large, seven are held in Arusha including Akayesu, four are in detention in Cameroon and the United States and Switzerland hold one each.
